title: Welcome to Thornbury Botanical Gardens
context: You will hear a volunteer guide talking to visitors at a botanical garden.

lines.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Thornbury Botanical Gardens. My name's Eleanor, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. Before you set off to explore on your own, I'll tell you a little about the gardens, and then I'll show you where everything is on the map you were given at the gate.

The gardens were opened in 1874. A lot of visitors assume they were created by a wealthy family, because of the grand iron gates, but in fact the land was bought by the town's university, which needed somewhere to grow plants for its medical students to study. The university still owns the gardens today, although they've been open to the public for well over a century.

Our opening hours have changed recently. We used to close at five o'clock all year round, but from this month we stay open until eight in the evening on Fridays and Saturdays during the summer, so you can enjoy the gardens after work. We do still close on Christmas Day, and we open at nine every morning, as before.

Entry to the gardens is free, as you know, but there are a few things you'll need to pay for. Guided tours of the glasshouse cost three pounds, and the audio guide, which used to be free, now costs two pounds. However, the children's activity booklet is still free, and you can pick one up at the visitor centre.

Just a couple of rules. You're very welcome to have a picnic on any of the lawns, and you can wheel bicycles along the main path, although please don't ride them. We do ask that you keep dogs on a lead at all times, because of the wildlife around the lake.

Right, if you look at your map, you'll see that we're standing just inside the main entrance, at the bottom of the map, on the southern edge of the gardens. The visitor centre is here, just to the east of the entrance, on your right.

First of all, if you turn left as soon as you come through the gate and follow the hedge all the way west, you'll reach the herb garden, which is right over in the south-west corner. It smells wonderful at this time of year.

Now, the main path runs straight north from the entrance, right through the middle of the gardens. Walk up it and you'll come to a crossroads, where it meets the path that runs from east to west. Just before you reach the crossroads, on your left, you'll find the café. On the opposite side of the main path, on the right, there's a first aid point, so if anyone feels unwell, that's where to go.

If you turn left at the crossroads and walk west, you'll see the lake on your right. Between the path and the lake, on the southern shore of the lake, is the Japanese garden, with its little wooden bridge.

Back at the crossroads, if you carry on north along the main path, right to the very end, you'll find the bird hide on your left. It sits between the path and the eastern edge of the lake, so it's perfect for watching the herons.

Alternatively, turn right at the crossroads and follow the path east, all the way to the end. Then look to your left, and you'll see the tropical glasshouse, up in the north-east corner of the gardens. The area beside the main path on that side, just north of the crossroads, is closed this year while we build a new rock garden, so please don't go in there.

And finally, the wildflower meadow. It's tucked away behind the visitor centre, that is, on its eastern side, close to the southern boundary of the gardens. It's at its best in June, so you've chosen a good week to visit.
Right, I'll be in the visitor centre until lunchtime if you have any questions. Enjoy your visit.
